lead: A turbine runner is a wheel with blades. Water enters at one radius and leaves at another. The blade moves, so the water's velocity seen from the ground and its velocity seen from the blade are different. A velocity triangle draws all three velocities at inlet and at outlet. Euler's turbomachine equation turns the change in the water's angular momentum into head and work. Every Pelton, Francis and Kaplan design uses these two triangles. The same equation, with signs reversed, gives the head a pump adds.
prereq: You need: the angular momentum equation from Unit 3, and relative velocity over a moving vane from 6.1.

sections.h3: The three velocities at one point

blocks.text: At any point on a runner blade, three velocities meet. The absolute velocity V is the water's velocity measured by a stationary observer, in m/s. The blade speed u is the velocity of the runner at that radius, in m/s. The relative velocity V_r is the water's velocity seen by someone sitting on the blade, in m/s. These three form a closed triangle: V = u + V_r as vectors. The blade speed follows the runner size and speed:

blocks.where: u is blade speed in m/s; D is the diameter at that point in m; N is runner speed in rpm.

blocks.text: Split V into two perpendicular parts. The whirl velocity V_w is along the direction of blade motion. The flow velocity V_f is at right angles to u, through the blade passage. Then V_w = V cos α and V_f = V sin α, where α is the angle between V and u. At inlet use subscript 1; at outlet use subscript 2 and draw a second triangle. The blade angles decide the shape. Water should enter without shock, so V_r1 should line up with the inlet blade angle. Figure 1 shows the inlet triangle for the worked example below.

Unit 3 gives the angular momentum equation: torque on the fluid equals the rate of change of its angular momentum. For a runner, T = ρQ(r₁V_w1 − r₂V_w2), where T is torque in N·m, ρ is density in kg/m³, Q is volume flow in m³/s, r is radius in m, and V_w is whirl velocity in m/s. The runner turns at angular speed ω = 2πN/60 rad/s, so power is P = Tω. Since u = ωr, P = ρQ(u₁V_w1 − u₂V_w2). Divide by weight flow ρQg to get head. This is Euler's turbomachine equation:

blocks.where: H_E is Euler head in m of fluid; u is blade speed in m/s; V_w is whirl velocity in m/s; g is 9.81 m/s²; subscript 1 is inlet, 2 is outlet.
w is work per unit mass in J/kg.

blocks.text: The equation is a difference, so the sign of V_w2 matters. If the outlet whirl is in the same direction as u₂, subtract. If the runner turns the water so that V_w2 points opposite to u₂, put V_w2 as negative; the two terms add. A good turbine tries to leave the water with little or no whirl, V_w2 ≈ 0, giving H_E = u₁V_w1/g. Never use the full V in place of V_w.

sections.h3: Degree of reaction and the pump sign

blocks.text: Degree of reaction R tells how much of the head is converted in the runner by falling pressure rather than by changing kinetic energy. R = (static pressure drop in the runner)/(total head across the runner). For an impulse turbine the pressure is the same on both sides of the runner, so R = 0. For a reaction turbine the pressure falls across the runner, so 0 < R < 1; a Francis runner typically has R around 0.5. Francis and Kaplan are reaction machines; see 6.5. A Pelton wheel is impulse with R = 0; see 6.4.

Euler's equation above is written for a turbine: the fluid gives energy to the runner, so work is positive out. For a pump the runner gives energy to the fluid. The same equation is used with inlet and outlet signs reversed: H_pump = (u₂V_w2 − u₁V_w1)/g. A pump therefore needs outlet whirl larger than inlet whirl. The full pump triangles, minimum starting speed and NPSH are in Unit 7.

spec.aria: Inlet velocity triangle for the worked example: O to A is u = 20 m/s, O to C is V_w1 = 21.65 m/s, C to B is V_f1 = 12.5 m/s, O to B is V₁ = 25 m/s, and A to B is V_r1 = 12.6 m/s.

examples.question: At the inlet of a turbine runner the blade speed is u₁ = 20 m/s. Water enters with absolute velocity V₁ = 25 m/s at 30° to the direction of blade motion. Find V_w1, V_f1 and V_r1. If the outlet whirl is zero, find the work per unit mass.
steps: Resolve V₁ along and across the blade motion: V_w1 = V₁ cos 30° = 25 × 0.8660 = 21.65 m/s.
Outlet whirl V_w2 = 0. Work per unit mass w = u₁V_w1 − u₂V_w2 = 20 × 21.65 − u₂ × 0 = 433 J/kg.
examples.answer: V_w1 = 21.65 m/s, V_f1 = 12.5 m/s, V_r1 ≈ 12.6 m/s, and with zero outlet whirl the work per unit mass is 433 J/kg.
examples.check:
import math
V1 = 25.0
u1 = 20.0
alpha = math.radians(30)
Vw1 = V1 * math.cos(alpha)
Vf1 = V1 * math.sin(alpha)
Vr1 = math.sqrt(Vf1**2 + (Vw1 - u1)**2)
w = u1 * Vw1
print(f'{Vw1:.2f}')
print(f'{Vf1:.1f}')
print(f'{Vr1:.1f}')
print(f'{w:.0f}')

traps: Using V instead of V_w in Euler's equation. Only the whirl component creates torque about the axis.
Putting V_w2 as positive when the outlet whirl is opposite to u₂. Opposite whirl is negative, so the two terms add.
Mixing head and work. Euler head is in metres; work per unit mass is in J/kg. Divide by g to go from J/kg to m.
Calling degree of reaction zero for a Francis runner. Impulse means R = 0; Francis is reaction, 0 < R < 1.
Forgetting that u changes with radius. Use u at the inlet radius for u₁ and at the outlet radius for u₂.

quiz.q: Define whirl velocity and flow velocity at a point on a runner.
quiz.a: Whirl velocity V_w is the component of absolute velocity along blade motion: V_w = V cos α. Flow velocity V_f is the perpendicular component: V_f = V sin α, where α is the angle between V and u.

quiz.q: Write Euler's head equation for a turbine and state the unit of each term.
quiz.a: H_E = (u₁V_w1 − u₂V_w2)/g. H_E is in m; u₁, u₂ and V_w1, V_w2 are in m/s; g = 9.81 m/s².

quiz.q: Why does a turbine runner aim for V_w2 ≈ 0?
quiz.a: The outlet whirl term vanishes. The exit water carries little swirl, so the leaving kinetic energy loss is small, and the Euler head is u₁V_w1/g. The gain is in efficiency, not in maximum head: a negative V_w2 would add to the head but would throw away energy in the exit swirl.

quiz.q: Explain why an outlet whirl opposite to u₂ increases the Euler head.
quiz.a: Euler's equation has −u₂V_w2. If V_w2 is opposite to u₂, it is negative, so −u₂V_w2 becomes positive. The outlet term adds to u₁V_w1 instead of subtracting from it.

quiz.q: A runner has u₁ = 15 m/s, V_w1 = 18 m/s, u₂ = 10 m/s, V_w2 = −2 m/s. Find the Euler head. Take g = 9.81 m/s².
A turbine has u₁ = u₂ = 12 m/s, V_w1 = 14 m/s, V_w2 = 0. Find work per unit mass and Euler head.
Two turbines have the same u and V_w1. Turbine A has V_w2 = +3 m/s; turbine B has V_w2 = −3 m/s. Compare their Euler heads.
quiz.a: B has the larger Euler head. The difference is [uV_w1 − u(−3)] − [uV_w1 − u(3)] = 6u in J/kg, or 6u/g in metres. The opposite outlet whirl adds to the inlet whirl term.

beyond: Not for the exam. CFD codes solve the flow equations (Navier–Stokes, or the inviscid Euler flow equations in a fast approximation) through each blade passage to predict efficiency before a runner is cast; the velocity triangles and Euler's turbomachine equation are then used to check the overall head and work. Blade designers search for shapes that keep V_r1 aligned with the blade and leave little whirl at outlet. The same angular momentum balance appears in wind turbines, compressors and torque converters. Search for 'Euler turbomachinery equation', 'velocity triangles reaction turbine' and 'blade loading coefficient'.
